before.description: How cells divide by mitosis and meiosis, plus osmosis, diffusion and active transport.
before.content_html:
The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells in your body divide to grow, repair damaged tissue and replace worn-out cells. This process follows a pattern called the cell cycle. Most of the cell cycle is spent in a growth phase called interphase, during which the cell’s DNA is replicated and the number of sub-cellular structures (organelles) increases.

Once the cell has copied all of its DNA and organelles, it enters mitosis. During mitosis, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell. The cytoplasm and cell membrane then divide to produce two genetically identical daughter cells. Each daughter cell has the full set of 46 chromosomes (in humans).

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. The cell cycle consists of interphase (growth + DNA replication) followed by mitosis and cell division.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and become specialised. In humans, embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell type, while adult stem cells (found in bone marrow) are more limited. In plants, meristem tissue retains the ability to differentiate throughout the plant’s life.

Stem cells have therapeutic uses — for example, treating paralysis or diabetes — but raise ethical concerns, particularly around the use of embryonic stem cells. You need to be able to discuss both the potential benefits and the ethical objections.

Diffusion

Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from a region where they are at a higher concentration to a region where they are at a lower concentration. It occurs in both liquids and gases and does not require energy. Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of cells by diffusion.

The rate of diffusion is affected by the concentration gradient (a steeper gradient means faster diffusion), the temperature (higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy), the surface area of the membrane and the distance the particles must travel.

Key Fact

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration. It is a passive process (no energy required). Factors affecting rate: concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance.

Osmosis

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a more concentrated solution (low water concentration). Like diffusion, osmosis is a passive process.

In Required Practical 3, you investigate the effect of a range of sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue. Potato cylinders placed in distilled water gain mass (water enters cells by osmosis) while those in concentrated sugar solution lose mass (water leaves cells).

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration. This requires energy from cellular respiration. Examples include root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from the soil and the absorption of sugar from the gut into the blood.

Active transport is essential when a cell needs to accumulate substances at a higher concentration than the surrounding environment. The energy for this process comes from the mitochondria.

Comparing Transport Methods

A common exam question asks you to compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport. Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy needed) and move substances down the concentration gradient. Active transport requires energy and moves substances against the concentration gradient. Osmosis specifically describes the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.

before.content_html:
Levels of Organisation

The human body is organised into a hierarchy. Individual cells with a similar structure and function are grouped together into tissues. Different tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together as organ systems. The digestive system is one of the main organ systems you need to know.

Key Fact

The hierarchy of organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. Each level builds on the one below it.

The Digestive System

The digestive system is a muscular tube running from the mouth to the anus. Its role is to break large, insoluble food molecules into smaller, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. Digestion involves both mechanical breakdown (teeth, churning in the stomach) and chemical breakdown by enzymes.

The main digestive enzymes are:

  • Amylase — produced in the salivary glands and pancreas; breaks down starch into sugars (maltose).
  • Proteases — produced in the stomach (pepsin), pancreas and small intestine; break down proteins into amino acids.
  • Lipases — produced in the pancreas and small intestine; break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.

Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine where it has two key functions: it neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach (creating alkaline conditions for enzymes in the small intestine) and it emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones to increase the surface area for lipase to work on.

Key Fact

Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and emulsifies fats in the small intestine. It also neutralises stomach acid to create the alkaline conditions needed by intestinal enzymes.

Enzymes and the Lock-and-Key Model

Enzymes are biological catalysts — they speed up reactions without being used up. Each enzyme has a specific active site with a unique shape. Only a substrate with the matching shape can fit into the active site, like a key in a lock. This is called the lock-and-key model.

Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and pH. If the temperature is too high or the pH is too extreme, the active site changes shape (denaturation) and the substrate can no longer fit. The enzyme stops working.

You should know the food tests for AQA Required Practical 2:

  • Starch — Iodine solution turns from brown-orange to blue-black.
  • Sugars — Benedict’s reagent heated; turns from blue to green/yellow/orange/red (depending on sugar concentration).
  • Proteins — Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple/lilac.
  • Lipids — Sudan III test; a red layer forms if lipids are present.

The digestive system demonstrates how organs work together as a system. The stomach churns food and adds acid; the pancreas produces enzymes; the liver makes bile; the small intestine absorbs soluble products into the blood; and the large intestine absorbs water.

before.content_html:
Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction that takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells. It uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The word equation is:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). It takes place in the chloroplasts and requires light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.

The rate of photosynthesis is affected by three limiting factors:

  • Light intensity — as light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until another factor becomes limiting.
  • Carbon dioxide concentration — increasing \(CO_2\) increases the rate until another factor limits it.
  • Temperature — higher temperatures increase the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions up to an optimum, beyond which enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply.

These limiting factors interact, and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis at a given time. Light intensity follows an inverse square law — it is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \frac{1}{d^2}\). You may need to explain graphs of photosynthesis rate involving two or three limiting factors simultaneously.

Plants use the glucose produced during photosynthesis for several purposes: respiration (to release energy), converting glucose to starch for storage, producing cellulose for cell walls, producing amino acids (by combining with nitrate ions from the soil) for protein synthesis, and producing lipids (fats and oils) for storage in seeds.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration is an exothermic reaction that takes place continuously in all living cells. It occurs in the mitochondria and requires oxygen. The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$$

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\). It is exothermic, occurs in mitochondria, and releases energy for life processes including muscle contraction, maintaining body temperature and building molecules.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is not available. It releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partially broken down.

In animals: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

In plants and yeast (fermentation): \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

During intense exercise, the muscles cannot get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so anaerobic respiration occurs alongside it. This produces lactic acid, which builds up in the muscles and causes fatigue and cramp. After exercise, you continue to breathe heavily to repay the oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed to break down the accumulated lactic acid.

Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.

During exercise, the body responds to the increased demand for energy: heart rate increases, breathing rate and depth increase, and blood is redirected to the muscles. These changes supply more oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration and remove more carbon dioxide.

practice_questions.text: State the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\) (1). Accept word equation for 1 mark if symbol equation not given.

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
practice_questions.marks: Aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not (1). Aerobic releases more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic / aerobic fully breaks down glucose (1). Accept: different products.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis reaches a plateau as light intensity increases.
practice_questions.marks: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases because more light energy is available for the reaction (1). At a certain point, another factor becomes limiting (e.g. CO2 concentration or temperature) (1). Increasing light intensity beyond this point has no further effect on the rate because another factor is now restricting it (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain what happens in the body during vigorous exercise to supply the muscles with more energy.
practice_questions.marks: Heart rate increases to pump more blood to the muscles (1). Breathing rate and depth increase to take in more oxygen and remove more CO2 (1). Blood is redirected from non-essential organs to the muscles (1). If oxygen supply is still insufficient, anaerobic respiration occurs alongside aerobic, producing lactic acid (1).

practice_questions.text: A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis by counting bubbles of oxygen produced by pondweed. At a distance of 10 cm, 60 bubbles were produced per minute. At 20 cm, only 15 bubbles were produced. Explain these results.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation linking inverse square law to rate.
As the distance from the light source increases, the light intensity decreases (1). Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance (1). At 20 cm, the light intensity is 1/4 of the intensity at 10 cm (1). Light is needed for photosynthesis, so a lower light intensity means a lower rate (1). Fewer oxygen bubbles are produced because less photosynthesis is occurring (1). The results show light intensity is a limiting factor at these distances (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to lactic acid after vigorous exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Lactic acid is transported by the blood to the liver (1). In the liver, it is broken down / converted back to glucose, which requires oxygen (oxygen debt) (1).

before.content_html:
Culturing Microorganisms

Microorganisms such as bacteria can be grown in the laboratory using nutrient media. This allows scientists to study how they grow, test antibiotics, and investigate disease. In the separate biology specification, you need to understand the practical techniques used to culture microorganisms safely and aseptically.

Key Fact

An aseptic technique is used to prevent contamination of bacterial cultures by unwanted microorganisms from the environment. This ensures that only the microorganism being studied grows on the culture medium.

To culture bacteria, scientists use either a nutrient agar plate or a nutrient broth. Agar plates provide a solid surface on which individual colonies can be seen, while broth allows bacteria to grow in liquid suspension.

Aseptic Technique Steps

To prevent contamination, a specific set of precautions must be followed during any work with microorganisms:

  • Sterilise all equipment (Petri dishes, inoculating loops) before use — an inoculating loop is passed through a Bunsen burner flame until it glows red.
  • Lids of Petri dishes are secured with tape but not sealed completely, to allow oxygen in but prevent contamination from above.
  • Work near a Bunsen flame to create an updraught that carries airborne microorganisms away from the open plates.
  • Incubate cultures at a maximum of 25 °C in schools (to reduce the risk of growing pathogens harmful to humans). In industry, cultures can be incubated at higher temperatures, often around 37 °C.

You may be asked to describe how to investigate the effect of antiseptics or antibiotics on bacterial growth. Paper discs soaked in different concentrations of antiseptic are placed on an inoculated agar plate. After incubation, clear zones called zones of inhibition show where bacteria could not grow.

The area of the zone of inhibition can be calculated using \(A = \pi r^2\), where \(r\) is the radius of the clear zone. A larger zone means the antiseptic is more effective at killing or preventing bacterial growth.

Plant Disease

Plants can be infected by a range of pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and protists. These diseases reduce crop yields and can devastate agriculture. You need to know specific examples and how to identify diseased plants.

Key Fact

Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) causes a mosaic pattern on leaves, reducing the area available for photosynthesis. There is no cure — infected plants must be destroyed.

Examples of Plant Diseases

Rose black spot is a fungal disease that causes purple or black spots on leaves. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop early, reducing the plant’s ability to photosynthesise. It spreads through water and wind and can be treated with fungicides or by removing and destroying affected leaves.

Crown gall disease is caused by the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which inserts its DNA into the plant cells and causes tumour-like growths (galls) on stems and roots.

Plant diseases can be identified by:

  • Stunted growth — nutrient deficiency or pathogen infection.
  • Spots on leaves — fungal or bacterial infection (e.g. rose black spot).
  • Areas of decay or rot — fungal or bacterial infection.
  • Discolouration — viral infection (e.g. TMV mosaic pattern) or mineral deficiency.
  • Malformed stems or leaves — viral infection or pest damage.

Gardeners and farmers can also use testing kits, laboratory analysis, or reference material to confirm diagnoses.

Plant Defence Responses

Plants have evolved physical, chemical, and mechanical defences against pathogens and herbivores:

  • Physical barriers: Cellulose cell walls, tough waxy cuticles on leaves, and bark on trees prevent pathogen entry.
  • Chemical defences: Some plants produce antimicrobial substances (e.g. mint and witch hazel) or poisons to deter herbivores.
  • Mechanical adaptations: Thorns, hairs, and leaves that droop or curl when touched deter herbivores.
Key Fact

Plants cannot move away from threats, so their defences must be structural or chemical. Some plants seal off infected areas by producing callose deposits to block the spread of pathogens through the phloem.
before.exam_tip_html: When asked to calculate the area of a zone of inhibition, always measure the diameter first, then halve it to find the radius before applying \(A = \pi r^2\). Show your working clearly and give units (mm²). Exam questions on aseptic technique often ask you to explain why each step is necessary — link every step to preventing contamination.

practice_questions.marks: A procedure/method that prevents contamination of cultures (1 mark) by unwanted microorganisms (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe how an inoculating loop is sterilised before use.
practice_questions.marks: The inoculating loop is passed through a Bunsen burner flame (1 mark) until it glows red hot (1 mark), which kills any microorganisms on it.

practice_questions.text: A student measured the diameter of a zone of inhibition as 14 mm. Calculate the area of the zone of inhibition. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks:
Radius = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 mm (1 mark)
A = π × 7² = π × 49 = 154 mm² (accept 150 mm² to 2 s.f.) (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explain why cultures in schools are incubated at a maximum temperature of 25 °C.
practice_questions.marks: At higher temperatures (1 mark) harmful/pathogenic microorganisms might grow (1 mark) which could be a health risk to students (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Compare the symptoms caused by tobacco mosaic virus and rose black spot fungus on infected plants.
practice_questions.marks: TMV causes a mosaic/discolouration pattern on leaves (1 mark) while rose black spot causes purple/black spots (1 mark). Both reduce photosynthesis (1 mark). Rose black spot causes leaves to turn yellow and drop, while TMV-infected leaves remain attached but with reduced chlorophyll (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Plants have evolved a range of defence mechanisms against pathogens and herbivores. Evaluate the importance of physical, chemical, and mechanical defences in protecting plants from disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed evaluation of all three types of defence, with specific examples and a clear judgement about relative importance.
Mid band (3-4): Description of at least two types of defence with some examples. May attempt comparison but without full evaluation.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description of one or two defence types with limited detail.
Indicative content:
• Physical: cell walls provide a tough barrier; waxy cuticle prevents pathogen entry; bark protects stems
• Chemical: antimicrobial substances kill pathogens (e.g. mint); poisons deter herbivores
• Mechanical: thorns prevent grazing; hairs deter insects; drooping leaves
• Physical defences are first line (always present); chemical and mechanical are more specialised
• All three work together as an integrated defence system

before.content_html:
What Are Monoclonal Antibodies?

Monoclonal antibodies are identical copies of one specific antibody. They are produced from a single clone of cells, so every antibody molecule is exactly the same and binds to the same specific antigen. This makes them extremely useful in medicine and research.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibodies are produced by stimulating mouse lymphocytes to make a specific antibody, then fusing those lymphocytes with tumour cells to create hybridoma cells that divide indefinitely and produce large quantities of the desired antibody.

Producing Monoclonal Antibodies

The production of monoclonal antibodies is a multi-step process:

  1. A mouse is injected with the target antigen. Its immune system responds by producing lymphocytes that make antibodies against that antigen.
  2. The antibody-producing lymphocytes are collected from the mouse’s spleen.
  3. These lymphocytes are fused with tumour cells (which divide rapidly and indefinitely) to form hybridoma cells.
  4. The hybridoma cells are screened to select those that produce the correct antibody.
  5. Selected hybridoma cells are cloned and grown in large quantities. They produce vast amounts of the identical monoclonal antibody.

Normal lymphocytes die after a short time outside the body. Tumour cells, however, divide uncontrollably and can survive indefinitely in culture. By fusing a lymphocyte (which makes the right antibody) with a tumour cell (which can divide forever), scientists create a hybridoma that combines both properties — it produces the correct antibody and never stops dividing.

Uses of Monoclonal Antibodies

Because monoclonal antibodies bind to one specific antigen with very high precision, they have a wide range of applications:

Pregnancy Testing

HCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin) is a hormone produced during pregnancy. Pregnancy test sticks contain monoclonal antibodies that bind to HCG in urine. If HCG is present, the antibodies trigger a colour change, producing a positive result.

Diagnosis of Disease

Monoclonal antibodies can detect specific molecules in blood or tissue samples. For example, they can identify the presence of a pathogen or a specific protein linked to a disease. In cancer diagnosis, monoclonal antibodies labelled with a radioactive tracer or fluorescent dye can bind to tumour-specific antigens, allowing doctors to locate tumours in the body through imaging.

Key Fact

In cancer treatment, monoclonal antibodies can be designed to carry a toxic drug, radioactive substance, or chemical directly to cancer cells. This is targeted therapy — it delivers the treatment only to the tumour, reducing damage to healthy tissue compared with chemotherapy.

Scientists use monoclonal antibodies to locate and identify specific molecules in cells and tissues. They can be tagged with fluorescent dyes, allowing researchers to visualise exactly where a particular protein is within a cell. This technique is invaluable in laboratory research for understanding cell biology and disease mechanisms.

Limitations and Ethical Concerns

Monoclonal antibodies were expected to be more widely used than they currently are. There are limitations:

  • They can cause unexpected side effects in some patients, which are sometimes more severe than the disease itself.
  • They are expensive to develop and produce.
  • They do not yet produce the miracle cures that were initially hoped for.

There are also ethical concerns about the use of animals (mice) in the production process, as mice must be injected with antigens to stimulate antibody production.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibody treatment is an example of targeted therapy because it delivers drugs precisely to diseased cells while leaving healthy cells unharmed.
before.exam_tip_html: Questions on monoclonal antibodies often ask you to describe the production process — learn the five steps in order. A common mistake is confusing hybridoma cells with normal lymphocytes. Remember: hybridoma = lymphocyte + tumour cell. If asked to evaluate their use, balance benefits (specificity, targeted treatment) against limitations (side effects, cost, ethical concerns about animal use).
